title: Every real primitive Dirichlet L-function has de Bruijn-Newman constant at most 9/32: a kernel-checked proof in Lean 4
description: Lean 4 sources, verification records and paper for the theorem that, for every real primitive Dirichlet character chi != 1 and every t >= 9/32, every zero of the de Bruijn-Newman heat flow of the completed L-function Lambda(s, chi) is real (classically Lambda_chi <= 9/32). The Lean theorem bb_real_primitive_meaning_oai is the conjunction of this statement with the identification Hchi chi 0 z = (1/8) N^((s+k)/2) completedLFunction chi s, s = 1/2 + iz/2, which says that the Lean heat flow is that of the classical completed L-function. It is proved in one environment (Lean v4.34.1, Mathlib d13f23b) with OpenAI's kernel-checked zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for Dirichlet L-functions (openai/math at adc7f124). Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound. The exported environment was replayed by five checkers from three implementation lineages (leanchecker, leanchecker-paranoid, nanoda, con-leche, con-ron), each of which rejected a skipKernelTC negative control; those replays were local and unsandboxed; a sandboxed Comparator run against a separately written challenge also accepted it. Reusable formal components: de Bruijn's theorem for a generic even kernel, Gauss's sign theorem for real primitive characters in Mathlib's normalisation, and the Mellin bridge from the theta kernel to Mathlib's completedLFunction. Credit: de Bruijn (1950, Theorem 13) for the engine; Freire, Gonzalez-Riquelme, Munoz, Poblete and Salinas (arXiv:2610.27343, Remarks 3.1 and 3.4) for the conditional statement Lambda_L <= D^2/2 = 9/32 under a zero-free strip of half-width 3/4; OpenAI for the 7/8 half-plane (manuscript unrefereed, Lean proof kernel-checked); Gauss for the sign theorem; Mathlib for the L-function API. Not a new analytic bound and not progress on the generalized Riemann hypothesis (Lambda_chi <= 0). Not yet refereed. Licensing: Lean sources and scripts Apache-2.0; paper and prose CC-BY-4.0.
